Minton date marks, 1842 to 1942

Minton impressed a small symbol beside its name each year from 1842 to 1942. Describe the symbol to find the year.

By Heirloom · Updated November 22, 2026

In short

A Minton year cypher is a small impressed symbol next to the impressed MINTON or MINTONS mark, a different one for each year from 1842 to 1942: an open triangle is 1843, an open square 1844. Many symbols look alike, so check the near matches before you settle on a year.

Find a Minton year cypher

Type a word for the small impressed symbol near MINTON or MINTONS. Every year whose cypher matches appears here, with the years it's easily confused with.

What the mark looks like

The impressed name, and a year cypher beside it. The photograph of the cypher is from a vase the Met dates to about 1867; its symbol, an A whose legs cross, is the cypher for that year.

Every Minton year cypher, 1842 to 1942

The descriptions are written from three published charts that agree on every year. Most pictures are cropped from the chart Frederick Litchfield printed in 1912 and again in 1925, which stops at 1907; where it differs from the table, the note under the picture says how. Five later cyphers simple enough to fix exactly are drawn; the rest have no picture yet. The symbols are small and often blurred by glaze, so match the overall shape and check the years in the last column.

Read these before you rely on a year

  • A date code only means something next to the right factory mark (impressed WEDGWOOD, impressed MINTON(S), the Royal Worcester printed mark, the Rookwood RP monogram, the Sevres interlaced Ls). A code alone does not identify the maker, and several of these systems were copied or forged (Minton by smaller makers; Sevres very widely).
  • The codes give a single year only when read exactly. Letters that look alike (I/J, U/V, O/Q, C/G) and blurred or glaze-filled impressions are the main source of error. When a reading is uncertain, report the candidate years.
  • All three charts (M1, M2, M3) agree on every year from 1842 to 1942. They appear to be copies of the same original chart (Godden's Encyclopaedia of British Pottery and Porcelain Marks), so they confirm the transcription but are not independent research.
  • The descriptions are our own words for each symbol, written after comparing the three charts. The symbols are small, impressed and often blurred by glaze, so match on overall shape. Use the confusable_with hints.
  • The cypher is impressed into the body and dates when the item was potted. Decoration can be later: M2 shows a item with the 1875 cypher that the artist signed in 1876.
  • Minton items can also carry an impressed month letter (e.g. S = September, O = October) and a potter's mark (M2, M3). These are not year marks.
  • Accept the cypher only with an impressed MINTON or MINTONS mark. M3 says some smaller makers copied the system. MINTON changed to MINTONS in 1871 (M2) or 1873 (M3); the sources disagree.
  • Sets that are easy to confuse: open triangle (1843) vs triangle with a circle (1878), triangle within a triangle (1879) and triangle with a vertical stroke (1880). Open square (1844) vs square with a dot (1869), square in a circle (1877), square quartered like a window (1881) and rectangle with an X (1884). X (1845) vs X with four dots (1855). Numbered shields 1-4 (1891-1894) vs numbered swans 1-6 (1895-1900) vs numbered circles 1-8 (1901-1908): read the outline as well as the number.
  • 1875 is drawn as a backward 3 (Greek epsilon) in M1 and M3, but on its side, like a lower-case m (two arches), in M2. Impressed marks can appear at any rotation.
  • The system ends with 1942 (a letter V). Minton used no year cyphers after that (all three charts stop at 1942).
  • The 1927 cypher is a swastika (hooked cross), as shown in all three charts. Describe it neutrally as the 1927 Minton year cypher.

Questions
